edits.find: He is not anorexic and he is not avoiding a food group — he is stuck on a texture. Advancing from purees to solids normally happens between 6 and 12 months, and failure to make that transition is the toddler's way of reporting dysphagia he cannot describe. The stem then removes the competing explanations one at a time: the swallow study is normal, so the problem is below the pharynx; development is normal, so this is not a behavioral or autism-spectrum feeding disorder; the stools are soft and daily with a benign abdomen, so it is not celiac disease or an intraabdominal process. What remains is inflammation of the esophagus, and the supporting clue is the one that reads like background history — eczema, because atopy accompanies most eosinophilic esophagitis. The diagnosis is histologic, so the test that establishes it is endoscopy with esophageal biopsy.
edits.with: He is not anorexic and is not avoiding a food group; he refuses a texture. Children normally advance from purees to solids between 6 and 12 months, and failure to advance in a toddler suggests dysphagia. The swallow study is normal, so the problem is below the pharynx. Because development is normal, a behavioral or autism-spectrum feeding disorder is unlikely. The stools are soft and daily with a benign abdomen, which argues against celiac disease or an intraabdominal process. That leaves esophageal inflammation. His eczema supports eosinophilic esophagitis, since most patients are atopic. The diagnosis is histologic, so the test is endoscopy with esophageal biopsy.

edits.find: "Has always been a picky eater" invites a behavioral reading and is the reason the stem bothers to say development is normal. The stool sentence is a planted negative doing real work: soft daily stools with no diarrhea or vomiting is what kills celiac disease and gastroenteritis. The eczema is the opposite of a decoy — it is the supporting evidence most readers skim past, because it arrives in the past-medical-history slot where decorative details usually live.
edits.with: "Has always been a picky eater" suggests a behavioral cause, but development is normal. Soft daily stools with no diarrhea or vomiting argue against celiac disease and gastroenteritis. The eczema, listed in the past medical history, is supporting evidence for eosinophilic esophagitis and is easy to overlook.

edits.find: A toddler stuck on purees with eczema and falling weight has eosinophilic esophagitis; endoscopic biopsy showing fifteen or more eosinophils proves it. · The shape of the refusal localizes the problem: a texture refusal points at the esophagus, a food-group refusal at celiac disease or an IgE allergy, and a poor appetite with normal eating at systemic or metabolic disease. · Eosinophilic esophagitis shifts its presentation with age — toddlers refuse solids, school-age children have abdominal pain and vomiting, adolescents get dysphagia and food impaction. · Atopy accompanies most cases, so eczema, asthma, allergic rhinitis or a known food allergy in a feeding-refusal stem is a clue rather than background. · The diagnosis is a cell count on biopsy, not a serology or a skin test; allergy testing guides the elimination diet only after the scope has settled the question. · Dietary elimination is first-line, with a proton pump inhibitor or a swallowed topical glucocorticoid as pharmacologic options, and feeding therapy for the avoidance the illness taught.
edits.with: A toddler stuck on purees with eczema and falling weight likely has eosinophilic esophagitis; endoscopic biopsy showing fifteen or more eosinophils confirms it. · The type of refusal localizes the problem: a texture refusal points to the esophagus, a food-group refusal to celiac disease or an IgE allergy, and a poor appetite with normal eating to systemic or metabolic disease. · Presentation varies with age: toddlers refuse solids, school-age children have abdominal pain and vomiting, and adolescents have dysphagia and food impaction. · Atopy accompanies most cases, so eczema, asthma, allergic rhinitis or a known food allergy in a child refusing food is a clue. · The diagnosis rests on the biopsy eosinophil count, not a serology or a skin test; allergy testing guides the elimination diet only after biopsy confirms the diagnosis. · Dietary elimination is first-line, with a proton pump inhibitor or a swallowed topical glucocorticoid as pharmacologic options, and feeding therapy for learned food avoidance.

edits.find: Fever, right lower quadrant tenderness, and a neutrophil-predominant leukocytosis are shared by both live answers, so none of them decides anything. Two findings do, and appendicitis can explain neither: twelve mucus-containing loose stools in 24 hours, and a brother with the same illness. What owns both is infectious ileocecitis — the pseudoappendicitis of organisms with an ileocecal predilection, Campylobacter jejuni and Yersinia enterocolitica. The migratory periumbilical-to-right-lower-quadrant pain, which reads as the appendicitis script, is in fact explained by the same answer: Campylobacter may infect the jejunum first and then spread to the ileum and cecum.
edits.with: Fever, right lower quadrant tenderness, and a neutrophil-predominant leukocytosis occur in both appendicitis and ileocecitis and do not discriminate. Two findings that appendicitis does not explain are twelve mucus-containing loose stools in 24 hours and a brother with the same illness. Both fit infectious ileocecitis (pseudoappendicitis) from organisms with an ileocecal predilection, Campylobacter jejuni and Yersinia enterocolitica. The migratory periumbilical-to-right-lower-quadrant pain also fits: Campylobacter may infect the jejunum first and then spread to the ileum and cecum.

edits.find: The brother is the most instructive detail in the stem, because it works in two directions at once: his existence supports an infectious cause, while his bloody stools invite the reader to assign Shiga toxin E. coli to a patient who has no blood in his own stool. A finding described in a contact is evidence about the exposure, not about this patient's phenotype. The migratory pain is the second trap and is subtler still — it is not inert, it is genuinely explained by the right answer, which is why it feels like confirmation of the wrong one.
edits.with: The brother's illness supports an infectious cause, but his bloody stools may prompt a diagnosis of Shiga toxin E. coli in a patient with no blood in his own stool. A contact's findings describe the exposure, not this patient's phenotype. The migratory pain is also explained by Campylobacter spread, so it does not confirm appendicitis.

edits.find: Appendicitis does not cause twelve mucoid stools and does not come with a sick sibling; ileocecal Campylobacter or Yersinia does both. · Profuse watery-then-mucoid diarrhea is what an appendix cannot do, and a sick contact is what an appendix cannot have; either one alone should stop the surgical reflex. · Campylobacter and Yersinia have an ileocecal predilection and therefore mimic appendicitis; imaging shows ileocecal inflammation and mesenteric adenopathy with a normal appendix. · Campylobacter may seed the jejunum before the ileum and cecum, which is exactly why the pain migrates like appendicitis.
edits.with: Appendicitis does not cause twelve mucoid stools or a sick sibling; ileocecal Campylobacter or Yersinia explains both. · Profuse watery-then-mucoid diarrhea or a sick contact alone should prompt reconsideration of appendicitis before surgery. · Campylobacter and Yersinia have an ileocecal predilection and mimic appendicitis; imaging shows ileocecal inflammation and mesenteric adenopathy with a normal appendix. · Campylobacter may infect the jejunum before the ileum and cecum, so the pain can migrate as in appendicitis.
